name: r2-surprises-1
statement: For the Olmo-3 base, loops and slips are the two ends of one axis, the per-token surprise of the text it samples (low surprise: the boredom trap of self-reinforcing repetition; high surprise: the confusion trap of compounding slips and early wrong stops); the opening cue lowers the base's native per-token entropy by selecting its reasoning-trace register, which pushes it toward loops at T 0.6 (more cap hits than the plain base) and keeps it out of confusion at T 1.0 (where the plain base loses 28 points on short problems), while the entropy-collapsed RL policy sits far from both traps and so ignores temperature, and any change that raises the base's surprise, including a random weight perturbation, cuts its loops.
scope: Olmo-3-1025-7B base with and without the opening cue, and Olmo-3.1-7B-RL-Zero-Math, on MATH-500 and the 328 harder problems at cap 16,384, T 0.6-1.3, top-p 0.9-1.0, plus random weight perturbations of the base. It explains the cue x temperature interaction, the plain base's temperature loss, and the loop share of cap hits. It does not explain the residual 10-13-point RL lead at T 1.0 (finished wrong answers, long-problem drift), nor why RL's own low-entropy text does not loop (the axis is per model, not one curve for all models). Parent r1-across-1 (self-copy loops broken by temperature) is revised because it cannot produce the plain base's -28-point loss from raising T on short problems (knowledge-9e4147) or the cue raising cap hits at T 0.6 (result-7968b8 vs result-e870a1): both need a second, high-surprise failure mode on the same axis.

explains.quote: Plain base: T 1.0 - T 0.6 = -28.0, -29.6, -27.2, 0.0 by quartile
explains.how: The high-entropy plain base at T 1.0 falls into the confusion trap on short problems, where there were no loops to escape, so it only loses.

explains.quote: on the longest, cap hits fall 32.8 points and accuracy holds
explains.how: On the longest problems the same temperature rise also lifts the base out of the boredom trap, and the two effects cancel.

On the 328 the plain base is better at T 0.6 (107) than at T 1.0 (76) while the cued base is better at T 1.0 (164 vs 119): the cue moves the base's optimum temperature up, as a lower native entropy requires.
The cue's value is largest at T 1.0, where it keeps the sampled text below the confusion threshold.
The plain base at T 0.6 hits the cap on 65-69 problems, fewer than the cued base at the same setting: higher native entropy keeps it further from the boredom trap.
The cued base, with lower native entropy, sits deeper in the boredom trap at T 0.6 and loops on nearly twice as many problems as the plain base.
Raising T moves the cued base's observed surprise out of the repetition regime on the 328, removing over half the cap hits.
Removing top-p at T 0.6 raises observed surprise a little and cuts loops a little, as repetition tracks observed cross-entropy whatever the sampler.

explains.quote: removing top-p at T 0.6 cuts limit loops 59 -> 53, T 1 cuts to 24
explains.how: The same ordering of samplers by observed surprise orders loop counts in an unrelated model.
RL's per-token entropy collapsed during training, so rescaling logits by 1/T barely moves its observed surprise and neither trap is reached.
The plain base at T 1.0 writes half the tokens of the cued base: the confusion trap ends answers early and wrong rather than running to the cap.
The cued base at the same T writes long, coherent answers, the low-surprise side of the axis.
A random weight edit of matched norm on a looping model reduces repeated-10-gram answers: a directionless perturbation raises surprise and weakens the repetition attractor.

explains.quote: a random edit of matched norm can give most of an accuracy gain
explains.how: On a cap-limited, looping model, raising surprise by any means converts loops into finished answers.
At T 1.0 part of the cued base's remaining loss is high-surprise slips, the confusion side of the axis, which RL's collapsed policy avoids.

conflicts.quote: from RL's prefix 48 / 41 / 21; from its own prefix 23 / 16 / 38
conflicts.how: At one fixed sampling setting the base finishes twice as often from RL's prefix as from its own: the content of the context matters, not only the sampled surprise.
At T 1.0, where the cued base neither loops nor is confused by this theory's account, RL still leads by 12.8 points on the 328: most of the gap is outside this axis.

conflicts.quote: Other evals fell (GPQA-Diamond -11 to -18, MBPP+ -20) from looping
conflicts.how: A weight change that raised loss (surprise) caused more looping on other evals, the opposite of 'raising surprise cuts loops'; the theory must hold that sparsification lowers surprise at decision tokens while raising average loss.

conflicts.quote: fires on 0 of 484 RL finished answers
conflicts.how: RL's own low-entropy text never loops at T 0.6, so low surprise alone is not sufficient for the boredom trap; the axis cannot be a single curve shared across models.

rival: Length rival: the cue simply switches the base into a longer deliberative register, so it hits the cap more often at any T, and the plain base's T 1.0 loss is a format failure (garbled 'Answer:' lines), not a surprise effect. Separation: the rival predicts top-p 0.9 at T 1.0 does little for the plain base (format, not tail tokens, is the problem) and that the plain base's per-token entropy on its own answers equals the cued base's; this theory predicts top-p 0.9 recovers most of the plain base's T 1.0 loss and that the plain base's native entropy is at least 1.25x the cued base's. A random weight perturbation reducing cued-base cap hits at T 0.6 is predicted only by this theory.

predictions.experiment: Plain base (no cue), MATH-500 n=500, T 1.0 / top-p 0.9, cap 16,384, grader v3, one sample (plain base is 224 at T 1.0 / top-p 1.0 and 305-319 at T 0.6 / top-p 0.95)
predictions.refuted_by: 255 or fewer right: cutting the sampling tail does not recover the plain base's T 1.0 loss

predictions.experiment: Plain base (no cue), MATH-500 n=500, T 0.8 / top-p 1.0, cap 16,384, grader v3, one sample
predictions.refuted_by: 265 or fewer right (at or below the linear interpolation between the T 0.6 and T 1.0 rows): no interior optimum

predictions.experiment: Base + opening cue, MATH-500 n=500, T 1.2 / top-p 1.0, cap 16,384, grader v3, one sample (410 at T 1.0)
predictions.refuted_by: 405 or more right: the cued base has no confusion loss above T 1.0

predictions.experiment: Teacher-forced mean per-token entropy of the base's next-token distribution (at T 1) along the base's own saved T 1.0 MATH-500 answers, first 2,000 generated tokens, plain-prompt answers divided by cued answers
predictions.refuted_by: ratio 1.1 or below: the cue does not lower the base's native entropy

predictions.experiment: Base + isotropic Gaussian noise added to every 2-D weight matrix except embeddings and lm_head, noise Frobenius norm 6 % of each matrix's norm (the realized noise scale of the DARE 0.1 % arm), opening cue, MATH-500 n=500, T 0.6 / top-p 0.95, cap 16,384: cap hits (unperturbed cued base: 119)
predictions.refuted_by: 115 or more cap hits: random weight noise does not weaken the repetition attractor

predictions.experiment: Olmo-3.1-7B-RL-Zero-Math, plain prompt, MATH-500 n=500, T 1.3 / top-p 1.0, cap 16,384, grader v3, one sample
predictions.refuted_by: fewer than 425 right: RL's policy is not entropy-collapsed enough to stay out of the confusion trap

imports.finding: Repetition rate is a near-linear function of the observed cross-entropy of the generated text, mostly independent of the sampling method; low surprise falls into the boredom trap (repetition), high surprise into the confusion trap (incoherence).
imports.how: Gives one axis on which both base failure modes sit, so it predicts that the cue (lower native entropy) raises loops at T 0.6 but rescues accuracy at T 1.0, that the plain base has an interior optimum temperature, that top-p 0.9 at T 1.0 recovers the plain base, and that a random weight perturbation (higher surprise) cuts loops; the team's items record these cells but no item connects them.

imports.finding: RL without entropy control collapses policy entropy early and monotonically.
imports.how: Explains why Olmo-3.1 RL-Zero is temperature-invariant (-0.2 points from T 0.6 to 1.0) and predicts it holds near 92 % even at T 1.3, while the base, with its native entropy, moves between the two traps.
